title: The Perfect Man: Eugen Sandow (Legends of the Past)
summary: A biography of Eugen Sandow, from the boy inspired by Greek statues to circus strongman, inventor of bodybuilding shows, promoter of weight training for women and men, and physical culture professor to King George V. NH holds him up as an anti-black-pill figure who told everyone they could look like him through discipline and exercise.
claims: Sandow (born Friedrich Müller, 1867) was a very active child, and seeing Greek and Roman statues in Rome made him decide to look exactly like them; that is still a valid motivation today
At 18 Sandow left Prussia to avoid conscription and worked as an artist's model; his body was used to recreate Greek proportions, e.g. a Lambeaux sculpture in a Belgian fine arts museum
Sandow was taken on by Professor Attila (Louis Durlacher) and took his stage name from his mother's maiden name
For free publicity Sandow broke strength-testing machines in Amsterdam; when arrested he broke one in front of the police, who then came to his show
Sandow looked small in clothes; he wore a tear-away suit to reveal his physique, and beat the strongman Samson on his own stage by lifting the same weight for more reps
Sandow's feats were built for spectacle: a bridge holding a plank that a horse walked across, and a pony 'carried overhead' that actually rested on his upper back as an assisted carry
Old-time strongman acts carried symbolism and a message; modern strongman is pure performance
Sandow coined the term bodybuilding and staged the first posing shows: standing on a box under a light, with powder or bronzing to look like a statue
At 5'8 and 185 lb, Sandow's balanced physique would still be a very good natural physique today; his chest and legs lagged
Sandow's sunken chest is explained by the lack of horizontal pressing at the time: no bench press or dips, and push-ups alone are not enough
Sandow was the first to show a crisp, defined six-pack; everyone has one lying dormant
Sandow trained with strongman lifts and his own dumbbell system; NH plans to turn it into a nucleus-overload circuit template
His 'lion tamer' act flopped when the old lion Commodore refused to fight, but stepping into a ring with a lion is still impressive
Thomas Edison filmed Sandow flexing in one of the first motion pictures, as the ideal human specimen
Sandow kept telling people anyone could become like him through discipline and exercise; he did not want fitness to be an elite club for the genetically gifted, anticipating today's black pill
Dudley Sargent of Harvard called Sandow the finest specimen of manhood he had ever seen
Train in front of mirrors and appreciate your flex: Sandow's 'mirror mood boost' raises confidence and motivation, and a little vanity is fine
Sandow encouraged women to lift weights; lifting makes women more feminine and men more masculine, and only exogenous male hormones make women look masculine
Sandow opened the Institute of Physical Culture in 1897 and ran judged shows with around 30 competitors; Arthur Conan Doyle judged and credited his neck training for surviving a crash
NH wishes modern leaders lifted like Theodore Roosevelt, who met Sandow and was an avid physical culturist
A great physique is a universal language that crosses borders and ethnic lines; we can all be brothers in iron
In 1911 Sandow became professor of physical culture to King George V; earlier he sold personal training plans by mail for $10, making him the first personal trainer
Modern pro bodybuilding no longer inspires people to train; its physiques are unrelatable and its audience is mostly non-lifters
Sandow wrote 'Life is Movement' to prepare people for war and trained British soldiers
Sandow is credited with turning yoga into a more exercise-based practice
War shut down his German-made products (including a grip dumbbell) and nearly bankrupted him; his family buried him in an unmarked grave and his name was later restored by a great-grandson
Sandow died at 58 of an aneurysm days after reportedly lifting his own car out of a ditch
Sandow was the perfect man not because of perfect genetics but because he proved excellence is achievable
exercises: bridge on hands and feet while a plank and horse cross the body
pony rests on the upper back, one arm locked on a harness
sold as a one-arm overhead lift
only horizontal press of Sandow's era; not enough to build a full chest
